content:
Black is more than the absence of color. It carries depth, mystery, power, and quiet elegance. In this post, you will explore over 100 shades of black, ranging from soft charcoal tones to intense jet black. Each shade may look subtle at first, yet every one has its own personality and story.

There are many colors that sit close to pure black. These shades keep hints of their original hue and saturation while staying very low in brightness. Well known examples include ebony, charcoal, onyx, jet black, and licorice, each offering a slightly different mood and visual weight.

For every shade, we include HEX, RGB, and CMYK codes, along with clear meanings and practical uses. By the end, you will understand how each black shade feels, where it works best, and how to choose the right one for design, art, branding, or decoration.

Black

Black is the absolute darkest color, representing the complete absence of light. Historically, it has been linked to power, elegance, and mystery. Ancient Egyptians associated it with fertility and the Nile’s soil, while in Medieval Europe, it became a color of solemnity and authority in clothing. Interestingly, achieving pure black dye was historically difficult and expensive, making it a status symbol. In design, Black is used for text, sleek interfaces, and to convey sophistication. It also carries meanings of mourning and the unknown in various cultures.

  • RGB 0, 0, 0
  • CMYK 0, 0, 0, 100

Jet Black

Jet Black is an extremely deep black, often described as blacker than black, with a namesake derived from the dense mineraloid “jet”. This mineral was popular in Victorian mourning jewelry after Prince Albert’s death. The color signifies formality, seriousness, and high technology. It is a staple in luxury goods, like pianos and electronics, to project a premium, flawless image. Furthermore, Jet Black is prevalent in automotive finishes for a sleek, polished appearance.

Charcoal Black

Charcoal Black is a dark grayish-black, mimicking the color of burnt wood. It is a neutral, grounding color associated with strength, resilience, and industrial aesthetics. This shade is less severe than pure black, offering more depth and warmth. Consequently, it is widely used in modern interior design for feature walls and furniture. Charcoal Black also appears in fashion as a versatile alternative to black, conveying professionalism and stability.

Matte Black

Matte Black is a flat, non-reflective black that absorbs light. This finish eliminates gloss and sheen, creating a subdued, modern, and stealthy effect. It gained massive popularity in consumer technology and automotive design for its sophisticated, fingerprint-hiding properties. Matte Black conveys a sense of understated power and contemporary edge. Therefore, it is favored for tools, luxury gadgets, and minimalist branding where visual noise is reduced.

Raven Black

Raven Black is a blue-tinged, glossy black inspired by the iridescent plumage of the common raven. This color has mythological ties to prophecy and insight in various cultures, often seen as a messenger. It embodies mystery, intelligence, and a connection to the natural world. In use, Raven Black adds a layer of depth and richness compared to neutral blacks. It is frequently found in cosmetics, such as nail polish and hair color, for its vibrant sheen.

Onyx

Onyx is a dark black with subtle brown or green undertones, named after the layered chalcedony gemstone. Historically used in carving and Roman cameos, it represents discipline and self-control. This elegant shade is linked to protection and eloquence in crystal lore. It is a popular choice for jewelry, decorative arts, and luxury accents. Onyx provides a softer, more approachable alternative to stark black in design palettes.

Licorice

Licorice is a warm, brown-based black reminiscent of the licorice candy root. This rich shade is associated with sweetness, indulgence, and a touch of vintage charm. It evokes memories of classic confections and old-fashioned apothecaries. In design, Licorice adds warmth and nostalgia to a palette, preventing it from feeling too cold. It is effectively used in food packaging, retro branding, and cozy interior design schemes.

This color is deeply connected to astronomy, dreams, and introspection. It is a preferred background in astronomy software and thematic storytelling. Moreover, Midnight Black is common in formal wear and luxury packaging for its deep, serene quality.

Obsidian

Obsidian is a volcanic glass black, often with a hidden translucency or sharp edge connotation. It was historically prized for making tools, mirrors, and ceremonial objects due to its sharpness. This color represents truth, protection, and razor-sharp clarity. In modern contexts, Obsidian denotes strength, precision, and cutting-edge technology. Consequently, it appears in tech branding, gaming peripherals, and sleek architectural elements.

Ink Black

Ink Black is a deep, permanent black directly modeled on traditional writing and printing ink. It carries centuries of association with knowledge, communication, and record-keeping. Before the digital age, this was the definitive color of the written word. Thus, it conveys permanence, authority, and legibility. Ink Black is the standard for printed text, formal typography, and classic tattoo art, symbolizing enduring ideas.

Coal Black

Coal Black is a dense, sooty black that references raw coal, a fossil fuel. This color is tied to the Industrial Revolution, power generation, and utilitarian strength. It evokes imagery of machinery, locomotives, and raw industrial energy. In design, Coal Black conveys a sense of gritty, functional robustness. Therefore, it is used in industrial branding, workwear, and designs aiming for an urban, no-nonsense aesthetic.

Carbon Black

Carbon Black is a pure, pigment black made from elemental carbon, like soot or char. It is one of the oldest known pigments, used in prehistoric cave paintings and Egyptian inks. This shade is the basis for black in printing and automotive tires. It represents purity of form and fundamental materiality. Consequently, Carbon Black is essential in manufacturing, product design, and as a key pigment in artist materials.

Ebony

Ebony is a dark black-brown named after the dense, prized heartwood of the ebony tree. Historically used for luxury furniture, piano keys, and ornamental carving, it symbolizes luxury, gravity, and sophistication. This rich color has warm undertones that differentiate it from cooler blacks. Ebony is associated with dignity and timeless beauty. It is frequently employed in high-end woodworking, musical instruments, and elegant interior decor.

Pitch Black

Pitch Black is an exceptionally dark black, likened to the tar-like substance “pitch”. It describes an absence of light so complete it feels tangible, often used in phrases like “pitch-dark”. This color embodies total obscurity, the unknown, and profound depth. It is used in astronomy to describe space and in literature to build suspense. Pitch Black is chosen for theatrical backdrops and immersive experiences where minimal light reflection is critical.

It carries a historical connection to hearths, industry, and domestic life. Soot Black is useful for creating weathered, vintage, or distressed visual effects. Thus, it appears in heritage branding, historical reproductions, and textured fabric dyes.

This color has an ethereal, softening effect when layered over other hues. In design, Smoke Black is used for shadows, gradients, and semi-transparent overlays to add depth without solidity. This practical, neutral color is associated with durability and the modern built environment. Asphalt is a grounding base in urban design and apparel. Therefore, it is a common choice for activewear, automotive themes, and architectural models to convey a realistic, metropolitan feel.

It carries a sleek, modern, and slightly industrial connotation due to its use in lubricants and batteries. Graphite is perceived as intelligent, precise, and contemporary. This shade is linked to machinery, weaponry, and the raw materials of construction. Iron Black is less about elegance and more about functional power. This conceptually profound color can evoke feelings of awe or existential contemplation. In design, it creates stark contrast and focuses attention. Void Black is used in scientific visualizations of space, minimalist art, and designs meant to feel infinite or unfathomable.

This color is synonymous with high-end, cutting-edge consumer electronics like phones and laptops. It conveys a sense of advanced, professional technology. This color is more dynamic and less static than a flat black, suggesting movement and change. It is used in atmospheric photography, dramatic artwork, and branding for intense experiences. This color is associated with geothermal energy, raw landscapes, and foundational strength. Unlike cooler blacks, Lava Black has an earthy, organic warmth. This color is linked to serenity, reflection, and the closing of the day. It is less about absolute darkness and more about a gradual deepening. This color embodies true wilderness darkness, solitude, and profound stillness. It is deeper and more absolute than a standard night sky, emphasizing the absence of a guiding light.
